passage: Lunch-break note, Ms Alka. I noticed Bhupen at the end of the bench with no tiffin today. His friend Yash slid his own box towards him. "Mum packed too much," Yash said, and carried on talking about cricket as if nothing had happened. Bhupen's ears went pink and he stared at the box. He said, "Thanks," softly, took one piece of paratha, and smiled a small, awkward smile. I stayed at my desk and did not step in. The next day Bhupen came with roasted chana in a twist of paper. "Have some," he said. Yash took a big handful and said it was tasty. Both boys looked pleased.

qa.q: What did Bhupen bring the next day?
qa.a: He brought roasted chana in a twist of paper.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when his ears went pink and he stared at the box?
qa.a: Probably awkward and embarrassed at being helped, along with gratitude, since he thanked Yash softly and smiled a small smile.

qa.q: What made it easier for Bhupen to accept Yash's food?
qa.a: Yash did not make a show of it and kept talking about cricket, so Bhupen could accept warmly and later share something of his own. 😊

qa.q: How might Yash have seen the moment when he slid his box over?
qa.a: As something ordinary, since he said Mum packed too much and carried on talking about cricket.

grounding: A child gratefully but awkwardly accepts a richer friend's tiffin and shares something of his own in return.
